title: SLA-aware Canary Policy Compiler
creator: Ava Chen
description: Build a compiler that converts high-level, user-facing canary rollout configurations into validated, executable rollout plans. The compiler should merge traffic-split schedules, SLA targets, guardrails (latency/error/regression thresholds), and auto-rollback policies into a deterministic plan consumed by the runtime router and the rollout controller. It must validate conflicts, surface explainable errors to the Console, and emit tracing metadata for observability.
background: Current rollout behavior is encoded ad-hoc across the Console UI, runtime routing rules, and the rollout controller. That has produced inconsistent behavior during edge cases (e.g., overlapping schedules, conflicting guardrails, and differing interpretations of 'grace windows'). This ticket scopes a canonical translator ("compiler") that provides a single source of truth for scheduled steps, constraints, and runtime safety checks.
acceptance_criteria: Users can submit a single canary YAML/JSON that includes: traffic steps, step durations, SLA targets (p50/p95 latency, error-rate), metric lookback windows, and auto-rollback rules.
Compiler validates config semantics and returns human-readable errors for conflicts (e.g., overlapping schedules, impossible SLA targets, or mutually-exclusive guardrails).
Compiler emits an executable plan consumed by rollout-controller v2 and the router, including per-step traffic tables and guardrail bindings.
End-to-end test: a staged canary deploy in staging that intentionally violates the configured guardrail triggers auto-rollback within the defined "detection window" and notifies Slack/channel.
Dashboard shows compiled plan, active step, enforcement decisions, and reason for any automatic rollbacks or pauses.
Unit tests cover edge cases: zero-duration steps, fractional traffic splits, simultaneous shadow routing, and priority resolution between global and per-variant guardrails.
design_summary: The compiler accepts a simple, opinionated DSL (YAML/JSON) that defines release parameters. It will run three phases: 1) normalization (expand shorthand and canonicalize step timings), 2) validation (SLA feasibility checks, detect overlap/conflict), 3) plan emission (per-step traffic matrix, guardrail hooks, observability instrumentation). Compiler will be implemented as a standalone Go microservice with an idempotent API and OpenAPI schema to reuse in Console and CLI.
dsl_example:
---
name: sla-aware-canary
variants:
  - model:v2
  - model:v3
schedule:
  - step: 1
    traffic: {v3: 5, v2: 95}
    duration: 15m
  - step: 2
    traffic: {v3: 25, v2: 75}
    duration: 30m
  - step: 3
    traffic: {v3: 60, v2: 40}
    duration: 1h
slas:
  p95_latency_ms: 250
  error_rate_pct: 0.5
guardrails:
  - name: latency-regress
    metric: p95_latency_ms
    direction: increase
    threshold_pct: 20
    window: 5m
    action: rollback
auto_rollback: true
validation_policies: Reject schedules where sum of traffic != 100% after normalization unless shadow traffic is explicitly allowed.
Reject SLA targets that are below observed production baselines by more than 10% unless overridden with justification.
Ensure that guardrail windows do not exceed step duration; warn if they do and auto-adjust to min(step-duration, window).
When global and variant-level guardrails conflict, prefer the more conservative threshold and annotate the plan with both sources.
runtime_integration_notes: Plan emission includes: per-step traffic matrix, enforcement hooks (webhook IDs), required metrics to evaluate guardrails, rollback policy id, and a unique plan_hash. Rollout-controller subscribes to plan updates via the compile-service webhook or polls compile-service by plan_hash. The router will accept explicit per-variant traffic sets for immediate enforcement during canary steps.
observability: Compiler must emit structured events to tracing (trace_id), metrics for compilation latency and validation error rates, and an audit log entry for every accepted plan. Console will display diffs between requested config and compiled plan with reasons for normalization.
migration_plan: 1) Implement compiler behind feature flag. 2) Add UI path in Console to preview compiled plan without applying. 3) Run a few internal canaries using compiled plans in staging. 4) Gradually flip runtime to consume compiled plans for new rollouts. 5) Backfill existing active rollouts with compiled plans when safe.
testing_plan: Unit tests for DSL parser and validation rules. Integration tests in CI that spin up rollout-controller v2 and a canary router emulator. Chaos tests: simulate delayed metrics, partial metric signal, and noisy baseline. Observability e2e: ensure console shows plan diffs and rollback reasons.
risks: Incorrect normalization could produce unexpected traffic splits leading to customer-visible regressions.
False-positive guardrail triggers if metric windows or baselines are misconfigured, causing unnecessary rollbacks.
Performance: compilation latency needs to be low (<200ms) for interactive console previews; long validations (e.g., heavy SLO checks) must be async or cached.
Backward compatibility with existing rollouts must be handled to avoid mid-flight behavior changes.
mitigations: Add conservative defaults and a preview step; require explicit "confirm" to apply compiled plan.
Implement a canary period in staging with synthetic workloads to calibrate guardrail sensitivity.
Cache compiled plans and expose a fast-path for preview requests that uses cached validations.
Provide a rollback-to-previous-plan API and a runtime safety net that enforces a max-percentage immediate rollback guard.
open_questions: What is the canonical source of baseline metrics for feasibility checks (Console-derived historical vs. time-series query at compile-time)?
Should we allow fractional traffic percentages (e.g., 0.1%) for extremely high QPS customers?
Do we expose manual tuning knobs for guardrail sensitivity in the Console or keep them advanced/hidden behind 'expertMode'?
